notes.metricNote: Euro per vehicle in service is the comparable rate: it divides the same billing by the vehicles the parts were sold for, so a fleet that grew no longer flatters a flat euro line. A rate can still move because the fleet moved rather than because the billing did, and the fleet column below is there to show which.

notes.norm: Every period here is divided by its own fleet. Two answers are drawn on purpose: the solid line is the per-period fleet, the dashed line is the one 2025 estimate, and where they disagree about direction that disagreement is the finding. In your selection the rate went from EUR 53 to EUR 53 per vehicle (+0.6%) while the absolute euro went +3.7%. On the single 2025 estimate the same two periods read EUR 52 to EUR 53 (+3.7%), which is the euro move restated as a rate rather than a rate that can move on its own. Over the whole span CY2023 = January to December 2023 to CY2025 = January to December 2025 the two denominators read +2.6% on the single 2025 estimate against -10.1% on each periodâ€™s own fleet. They disagree about the direction, so which denominator is used is not cosmetic: the flat one is only the euro move, and the per-period one is the rate a reader can compare between periods. What the 2025 denominator is made of, from the workbookâ€™s own rows: ITUK 22,191 on the LD row, ITUK 877 on the F-series row. Where the denominator comes from. Both are read from the vehicle-in-service workbook. The single estimate is the modelâ€™s own three-way split, one vintage labelled 2025E; it is the second option in the control above and it stays on the page, because a reader should be able to check what the flat answer was rather than be told it was wrong. The default is the workbookâ€™s own count for the period, summed from the rows that name a vehicle type (the LD and MD rows are the N-series truck, the F-series row the heavy truck and the light-commercial row the light vehicle). Two defects in that source are carried here, not hidden. LD is a label, not a weight class: 6.5/7.5 t in Israel and about 3.5 t in most of Europe, two different parts spend rates on one label. The band is read per market, from the market's own measured 3.5 t share, never assumed. Open issue LD-LABEL. Israel's CV rows run about 25% LOW in every year against the Israeli ministry's own registrations, so a per-truck figure on UTI is flattered by an understated denominator. Open issue UIO-FCAST. Forward periods are not measured. 2026 to 2030 are forecast, not measured: the workbook scraps about 3% a year from 2026 while the 1990-2025 history uses a survival curve implying about 10.2% (trucks) and 12.3% (light vehicles), so the forward years are overstated by +9% in 2026 rising to about +59% by 2030 network-wide and worse per market. Open issue UIO-FCAST. The billing runs from January 2023, so a period later than 2025 would be a forecast denominator with nothing to divide, and those periods are excluded from the chart rather than shown as a fall.

notes.target: This is our own target, not an industry benchmark. A target spend per vehicle exists for 2025 and for the part-year 2026 only. A year with no target is shown without one rather than back-filled. The target is per market, so it shows where the gap between what we billed per vehicle and what a vehicle in that market is worth is widest; it does not say what share of that marketâ€™s parts demand we hold. A market with no dashed line has no target on disk for the period shown.
